job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Aaron Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up around eight in my parents' flat in Marlow Bridge and sit at the kitchen table with my laptop. I check the graduate boards, tailor a cover letter, and send maybe two applications. After lunch I help my sister Sana with her maths homework, then I walk to the library so I'm not staring at the same wall all day. It's been seven months since I finished, and I've sent about sixty applications.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was your degree, and what did the internships teach you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did accounting and finance, and I finished top of my year. One internship was in payroll at the city bus company, and the other was tax returns at a small firm called Hartley and Pryce. Payroll taught me how many people live pay cheque to pay cheque. Tax taught me that most of the work is checking numbers against rules, which I'm good at, but I also see how a program could do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, which we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief, honestly, because it means the hype was oversold. Some routine reconciliation work gets automated, and the rest of us carry on. I'd tell my friends the real problem is how few entry-level jobs firms advertise, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried, because my problem is right now. I have some debt, about two months of savings, and no offer, so a quiet world doesn't pay my loan. My dad keeps saying the market will pick up in spring, but he said that last spring too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, around ten a week, and stop only picking big firms. I'd ask Hartley and Pryce whether they'd take me on for the busy season, even short-term. I'd also join the local graduate union branch, because a group of us asking questions gets further than one of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, mostly. It's not fear of robots, it's the feeling that every no letter is a small vote against my four years of work. I get through it by walking and by helping Sana, who thinks I'm the clever one in the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've sent sixty applications. Where do you think the problem actually is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it is the market and some of it is the way firms use online forms. A program rejects you before a person sees your name, and nobody tells you why. Mum says maybe I'm too picky, but I've applied to everything within an hour's train ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've avoided AI tools so far. Is that a choice or a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a choice, mostly. I've seen the tools write confident nonsense, and in accounting a confident error is the worst kind. I'm not against learning, but I'd want to see them proven and I'd want to know who is accountable when they get something wrong.

say: I'd tell friends that **hype** always fades and the real issue is the shortage of entry-level jobs.
I'd say firms should stop hiding behind software and actually answer **applicants**.
think: Privately I'm still worried, because my **debt** and empty inbox don't care whether AI is hype.
I suspect firms use the slow market as an excuse to hire fewer **juniors** than they need.
do: Send about **ten applications** a week to smaller firms, not just the famous ones.
Ask Hartley and Pryce about **seasonal work** in their tax rush.
Join the local graduate **union branch** to compare notes and push for fair hiring.
feel: **Tense** and tired, but not frightened of the technology itself.
S0.quote: A program rejects you before a person sees your name, and nobody tells you why.
fieldNote: Aaron's worry is the present job market, not AI; he used the quiet scenario to talk about **rejection by forms**.
He blames employers and hiring systems, not himself, which fits his progressive, union-leaning view.
Resistance to AI tools is a reasoned stance about **accountability**, not ignorance.

steps.text: Send ten applications a week to smaller accounting firms
Ask Hartley and Pryce for seasonal tax-rush work
Join the local graduate union branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a rewrite of the entry level. Checking, reconciling and filing are what juniors do, and that's exactly what gets taken first. I'd tell people that companies should be required to say publicly how many junior posts they cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my path just got narrower. The easy first job I trained for, the one where you learn by checking other people's numbers, is the one most likely to shrink. I'm top of my class, but so are a lot of others, and fewer chairs means someone sits on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen the search to public bodies and charities, because they still hire people to be accountable, not just fast. I'd put aside a fixed hundred a month from the odd tutoring I do, and I'd write to my local councillor asking what the area is doing for graduates. And yes, I'd finally learn a spreadsheet automation tool, even if I don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty anxious. It feels like running up an escalator that's going down, and I can't see who is meant to be holding the rail. My parents keep saying I'm clever, which helps and also adds pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own skills do you think the software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reconciliation, categorising invoices, and the first draft of a tax return. Those were most of my payroll internship. The part software can't easily do is explaining a number to a worried client, and I'm not sure firms will pay a junior for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at your internships would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My supervisor at the bus company, Mrs Okafor, who has three payroll clerks and a boss who keeps asking how many she needs. She trained me patiently. I'd worry she's told to do the same with two, and the one who goes is the one on the temporary contract.

say: I'd tell people that **junior posts** are the first to go, and firms should publish how many they cut.
I'd say governments need to fund **retraining** before the damage is done.
think: I think my **first-job route** is getting narrower, even with top grades.
I'm uneasy about relying on tools I don't trust, but I can see I may have to.
do: Widen the search to **public bodies** and charities that still hire people to be accountable.
Put aside **a hundred a month** from tutoring as a cushion.
Write to my **local councillor** and learn one spreadsheet automation tool, reluctantly.
feel: **Anxious**, like running up a down escalator, with my parents' pride adding pressure.
S1.quote: The easy first job I trained for, the one where you learn by checking other people's numbers, is the one most likely to shrink.
fieldNote: He ties the threat to specific tasks from his internships, which makes it credible rather than generic.
Turns to **public-sector** jobs and the councillor, showing his instinct to seek institutional answers.
First hint of softening on tools, but reluctant and framed as necessity.

steps.text: Apply to councils, charities and public bodies that hire accountable staff
Put aside a hundred a month from tutoring
Write to my local councillor about graduate jobs
Learn one spreadsheet automation tool this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political emergency, not a personal failing. Two years isn't enough for any school, union or government to move, so I'd want an emergency summit and an income guarantee. I'd post that and go to whatever march gets organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think accounting as I trained for it ends before I've started. Everything I was good at, checking and reconciling, becomes something a machine does cheaper. I'd lie awake doing the maths on my loan, which has about fourteen thousand left, and on how long two months of savings lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop planning a ten-year career and take any job that pays, even warehouse hours, to cover the loan. I'd move my savings somewhere boring and not spend a penny. And I'd join every group I can, because on my own I have nothing to bargain with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. It's like hearing the factory I trained for is closing, and I didn't even get to work there. Part of me is angry that the people who built it are the ones who'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your parents the night it's announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with them and say I'm not going to panic, but I need them to know the plan is different now. Dad would say tough it out, Mum would cry, and Sana would ask if she should still do her exams. I'd tell Sana yes, always yes, because I don't want her to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop treating a graduate scheme as the goal and treat it as luck. I'd look at care work, public service, anything where people still want a person. I hate saying it, because my degree was meant to be the safe route my parents never had.

say: I'd call it a **political emergency** that needs an income guarantee, not personal blame.
I'd say people should join unions and **march** because one person alone has no bargaining power.
think: Privately I think the accounting career I trained for **ends before it starts**.
I'm angry that the people who built it will be fine while graduates carry the **debt**.
do: Take **any paid job**, even warehouse shifts, to cover the loan within weeks.
Move my savings into a **safe account** and stop all non-essential spending.
Join **every group** that organises, because alone I have no bargaining power.
feel: **Alarmed** and angry, with a sense of grief for the career my parents hoped for.
S2.quote: Everything I was good at, checking and reconciling, becomes something a machine does cheaper.
fieldNote: Strongest scenario for Aaron; he sees **no time** for any institution to respond, so his mood hits alarmed.
His grief is about his parents' hopes as much as his own money.
Plans are defensive and collective: cash, any job, **organising**.

steps.text: Take any paid job, even warehouse shifts, to cover the loan
Move savings into a safe account and stop non-essential spending
Join the union branch and every graduate organising group
Back an income guarantee by writing to my representative

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to bargain if we start now. Governments could pass rules on notice periods and public retraining, but only if people push. I'd tell friends to stop assuming somebody else will handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra time makes me less panicked but more resentful. I can see it coming, so no one can say they were surprised, and still it feels like nobody is acting. I could finish a professional exam or two and be a chartered accountant for a couple of years, but whether that's worth anything by 2031 I can't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the best entry job I can get, keep my head down and learn the work properly. I'd start the chartered exams on the employer's money if they pay, because that's a real exam and a person has to sign it. And I'd keep paying down the loan hard for the first three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but it has a shape now. I know what I'm doing this year, and what I'm watching for next year. The scary part is that every year someone says it's still coming and nothing's ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years change for you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm only reacting. With five years I can try and become the person who signs and explains things, which is harder to automate. It also gives the union time to win something, if people join.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you put your effort first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job first, because I can't do anything on no income. Then the exams, then the politics, in that order. I'll try to do all three, but if I'm tired, the politics goes last, and that's a thing I don't love admitting.

say: I'd tell friends that five years is enough to **bargain** if we organise now.
I'd say nobody should assume someone else will **handle** the change.
think: The extra time makes me less panicked but more **resentful** that nobody is acting.
I think being the **person who signs** and explains numbers may last longest.
do: Take the best **entry job** available and learn the work properly.
Start **chartered exams** on an employer's money, since a person must sign those.
Pay down the **loan** hard for three years.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a shape to it, because I know what to do each year.
S3.quote: With five years I can try and become the person who signs and explains things, which is harder to automate.
fieldNote: Time converts panic into a **sequenced plan**: job, exams, then politics.
Resentment, not fear, is the lead emotion; he feels the warning is wasted without public action.
Honest about politics being what drops first when he's tired.

steps.text: Accept the best entry-level accounting job offered
Start chartered accountancy exams on the employer's money
Put extra every month towards the student loan
Keep attending the union branch meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say we have time to do it properly, with retraining paid for and rules in place. I'd say that's where unions earn their place. If we waste it, it'll be our fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more settled, because ten years is a whole career stage. I could get the first job, qualify, and maybe move into advisory work where people still want a person. I'd still worry for people my age, because the first jobs would be thinning from now on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply as I'm doing now, but with less panic. I'd get qualified, and probably learn the tools a bit at a time, maybe by 2029, when I can see which ones hold up. I'd save for a flat deposit, which I couldn't imagine with a shorter timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than with the others, but not carefree. It still feels uncertain because I can't plan a family or a flat around a date nobody can confirm. I think I'd feel guilty relaxing while others struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a decade that you can't do with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade lets me qualify and build a track record before the squeeze. It also lets governments act, if people vote for it. With two years I'd just be surviving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust this timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I trust it as much as any forecast, which is not much. Experts have said it was close for years. I'd still plan as if it's real, because if I'm wrong, I only lose a bit of caution.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to do it **properly** if governments and unions use it.
I'd say we'd have only ourselves to blame if the time is **wasted**.
think: Ten years is a **whole career stage**, so I could qualify and move into advisory work.
I still worry for **graduates my age**, because entry-level jobs thin out first.
do: Keep applying now, with less panic, and **qualify** as an accountant.
Learn AI tools gradually from about **2029**, once I see which survive.
Save towards a **flat deposit**, which I can't imagine under the shorter timelines.
feel: **Calmer**, but a little guilty relaxing while other graduates struggle.
S4.quote: I can't plan a family or a flat around a date nobody can confirm.
fieldNote: Longest timeline brings the most **settled** Aaron, though the current no-offer pressure keeps it at uneasy.
He plans to adopt tools late and only when proven, which fits his resistant profile.
Guilt about relaxing shows his collective instinct.

steps.text: Keep applying while working towards the accounting qualification
Try one AI tool a year from 2029 once proven
Save a flat deposit from the first salary

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because two years is nothing and I'd be competing with everyone else who got cut at once. What would help is a proper public plan: retraining paid for by the state, rules on how fast firms can replace staff, and unions at the table. I'd also want somebody to pay me while I work out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me get told to just learn the tools. I'm not scared of learning, but I haven't been given a reason to trust the tools, or the companies selling them. I'd like the people choosing to automate to be the ones answering for what happens to us.

headlineQuote: My degree was meant to be the safe route my parents never had.
portrait: **Aaron** is a 23-year-old accounting graduate, top of his class, still without an offer after seven months of applying.
He lives with his parents and his sister, carries **some debt**, and has about two months of savings.
He is progressive, trusts **unions and public help** more than firms, and avoids AI tools on principle.
Across the five worlds he sticks with the familiar and looks to **collective action** and politics, not personal reinvention.
His mood climbs to alarmed only when time is shortest, because he sees no plan and no cover.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because two years leaves no time for retraining or public plans.
whatWouldHelp: A **state-funded retraining income** and rules limiting how quickly firms can replace staff.
A real seat for **unions** in deciding how AI is brought in.
